chunks: And as for what Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal narrated from Ali ibn Asbat, from al-Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked him about the dowry (mahr), when does it become obligatory? He said: When the curtain is lowered and the door is closed firmly.

He said: I married a woman during the lifetime of my father Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him), and my soul longed for her, so my father forbade me, saying: Do not do it, O my son, do not go to her at this hour. But I insisted on doing so. When I entered upon her, I threw a cloak that was on me towards her, and I disliked her, and I went to leave. Then a female slave of hers stood up, lowered the curtain and closed the door firmly. I said: Stop, for what you want has become obligatory.

So this narration does not negate the reports we have previously mentioned, because in the narration it is not stated that the dowry became obligatory. Nor is it impossible that he meant 'what you want has become obligatory' referring to settling with her over something she is pleased with.

And even if it mentioned the dowry, it would not mean that the thing that made the dowry obligatory was lowering the curtain and secluding with her. Rather, it is not impossible that he (peace be upon him) made it obligatory upon himself as a voluntary gift, without it being obligatory in principle.

And that which indicates this is that it has been narrated in this exact case that his father Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) said to him: She has only half the dowry. This indicates that if he gave her the entire dowry, he only gave it as a voluntary gift.
ai.seo_question: When does the full dowry become obligatory in Shia Islam according to the hadith of Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani's *al-Istibsar* illustrates the juristic nuance between legal obligation (*wujub*) and voluntary bestowal (*tabarru*) regarding the full dowry upon seclusion (*khalwah*). The Imam clarifies that while lowering the curtain and closing the door triggered his specific action, it did not necessarily establish a binding legal rule, as his father Ali ibn al-Husayn had previously advised him that only half was due, suggesting the full amount was given voluntarily to ensure satisfaction. This distinction is crucial in Shia fiqh for determining whether the full mahr is owed in cases of consummation versus mere seclusion.
